title: Covenant vs. Contract: What Marriage Actually Is
excerpt: A contract protects you from the person across the table, and a covenant binds you to them, which is why the modern wedding is a contract dressed in the language of a covenant it no longer believes.
body:
A woman I had married eleven years earlier sat in my office and told me she wanted out, and the reason she gave was that she was no longer happy. She was not lying. She was not even wrong about her own interior weather. She had simply absorbed, the way all of us absorb the air, an account of marriage in which her happiness was the thing the marriage existed to produce, and when it stopped producing it she concluded the machine was broken. I did not argue with her about her feelings. I argued with her about her categories. Because the trouble in that office was not that her marriage had failed. The trouble was that she and the man she married had never agreed on what marriage was.

This is the question underneath almost every conversation I have about marriage, and almost no one asks it directly. We argue about roles and finances and chores and whose family ruins which holiday. We do not argue about ontology. We assume we know what the thing is, and we assume the person across the bed assumes the same, and we are wrong on both counts. So I want to ask the question that the arguments are standing on. What is a marriage. Is it a contract, an arrangement between two parties for mutual benefit, dissolvable when the benefit dries up. Or is it a covenant, a binding of two lives under a promise that does not depend on the benefit at all.

## The Case Against the Vow

The honest skeptic has a strong case here, and I want to put it at its strongest before I answer it, because the version of the case I can defeat easily is not the version anyone actually holds. The skeptic says the covenant talk is a trap. For most of human history, he says, marriage was an unbreakable bond, and what that unbreakability produced was not glory but captivity. Women could not leave men who beat them. People stayed thirty years in cold contempt because the promise was a cage and the culture welded it shut. The contract model, the skeptic continues, is not a moral decline. It is a moral correction. It says two adults enter freely, set terms, and retain the dignity of exit. The ability to leave is what makes the staying mean something. A love that cannot leave is not love. It is hostage-keeping with good lighting.

I think that argument is partly right, and I am not going to pretend otherwise to make my job easier. The history is real. The cage was real. There were and are marriages that should end, and a theology of marriage that cannot say so is a theology that has made an idol of an institution and fed people to it. Any account of covenant that I give has to be an account that protects the abused before it protects the institution, or it is not worth the paper. So I grant the skeptic his history and his outrage. What I do not grant him is his conclusion. Because the contract he offers as the cure does not actually deliver the dignity he promises. It delivers something else, and to see what, you have to watch what a contract is for.

## What a Contract Is For

A contract exists to protect each party from the other. That is its genius and its whole purpose. When I sign a contract, I am preparing for the moment the other party fails me. I am specifying, in advance, what I am owed and what I will do if I do not get it. Every contract is written with one eye on the exit. This is not cynicism. It is prudence, and in commerce it is exactly right. But notice what it does to the people inside it. A contract keeps the two parties separate. It defines where you end and I begin. It guards the self. And a marriage built on that logic will do exactly what it was built to do, which is keep two selves intact and adjacent, each watching the ledger, each measuring whether the benefit still exceeds the cost. The contract did not fail those couples. It performed flawlessly. It kept them safe from each other right up until it released them from each other. The skeptic wanted the contract to give him intimacy with an exit. But intimacy is the surrender of exactly the self-protection the contract is engineered to preserve.

> It kept them safe from each other right up until it released them from each other.

## One Flesh, and What It Cost

Let me carry one text through the rest of this, because I do not want to argue from sentiment. In the second chapter of Genesis, after the man has named every animal and found among them no counterpart, God makes the woman, and the man says she is bone of his bone and flesh of his flesh, and the text steps back from the scene to tell us what it means. Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh (Genesis 2:24 ESV). I want you to see the strangeness of that sentence. It does not say they shall cooperate. It does not say they shall meet each other's needs. It says they shall become one flesh, a single thing where there were two, a new and indivisible reality. That is not the language of contract. You cannot become one flesh with a counterparty. The whole grammar of contract depends on the parties staying two. Genesis is describing the precise thing a contract is designed to prevent.

And here is what most readers miss. The text says a man shall leave his father and his mother. In the world that produced those words, leaving your father and mother was not a Tuesday. It was the dismantling of your entire security. Your father's house was your economy, your protection, your name, your safety net. To leave it was to walk away from the only insurance you had. The covenant of marriage begins with an act of deliberate vulnerability, the surrender of your prior protection in order to be joined to another person. The contract begins with the opposite move. It begins by keeping your protections in place and writing down the conditions under which you will retreat into them. So we have two accounts of marriage that are not two flavors of the same thing. They are opposites at the root. One says hold fast and let your defenses fall. The other says stay guarded and keep the exit clear.

## How the Home Became a Haven

Now, how did we get from the one to the other, because we did not always live this way, and the shift has a history with dates and causes and names. For most of the agrarian world, the household was a productive unit. The married couple was a working partnership that grew food, made cloth, raised animals, and produced nearly everything the family consumed. Wendell Berry has spent a career describing this and grieving its loss. Marriage, Berry argues, was a form, a practiced shape that joined two people to each other and to a place and to the work that place required, and the love in it was not the cause of the bond but the fruit of the shared labor (Berry 1992). The household was where the economy and the affections were the same thing. You did not marry to be happy. You married to make a life, and the happiness, when it came, came as a byproduct of the life made.

That world did not end gradually. It was disassembled, and the disassembly accelerated sharply in the nineteenth century as industrial production pulled work out of the home and into the factory and the office. The household stopped producing and started only consuming. The husband left in the morning to earn money in a world the wife never saw, and the home was reinvented as the place he returned to, a refuge from the market rather than a partner in it. Christopher Lasch named this with a precision that has not aged. The family became a haven in a heartless world, a private retreat charged with supplying all the warmth that the public economy had stripped out of daily life (Lasch 1977). And here is the weight of his argument. The home could not bear that assignment. Asked to be the sole source of meaning, emotional repair, and personal fulfillment that an entire society had drained from work and community, the family buckled under a load it was never built to carry. We did not ask too little of marriage. We asked it for everything, and everything is more than any two people can supply.

Watch the line that runs from that reorganization to the woman in my office. Once the home became the haven, marriage became, by definition, the place you go to be fulfilled. And once that is what it is for, the contract logic is not a corruption of the model. It is the model finishing its own sentence. If the marriage exists to make me happy, then when it stops, it has failed its purpose, and a sane person exits a failed instrument. The no-fault divorce statutes that spread across the states in the 1970s, beginning in California in 1969, did not invent this. They ratified it. They wrote into law what the culture had already decided about what marriage was for. The contract did not break the covenant. The covenant had already been quietly redefined into a contract, and the law simply caught up.

## The Lost Grammar of the Vow

I want to slow down on one word, because the shift I am describing is buried inside it. The older world spoke of marriage as a vow, and a vow is a strange and almost archaic kind of speech. When you vow, you are not predicting your future feelings. You are binding your future self in advance, against the day your feelings argue otherwise, precisely because you know they will. A vow is a promise made by the present self to govern the future self when the future self would rather not be governed. That is its entire function. It exists to hold you when nothing else will, when the warmth is gone and the benefit has thinned and every honest feeling in you is voting to leave. The reorganization of the household did not merely move work out of the home. It dissolved the very idea that a person could bind his own future, replacing the vow with the preference, and a preference, unlike a vow, is by definition revisable the moment it stops preferring. Once marriage became a preference rather than a vow, its dissolution was not a tragedy requiring explanation. It was a preference simply changing, which requires no explanation at all. The woman in my office was not breaking a vow. In her own categories she had never made one. She had expressed a durable preference at a wedding, and the preference had run its course, and a preference that has run its course is not betrayed when it ends. It is merely concluded.

So when the skeptic offers me the contract as liberation, I want to tell him the truth as I see it. The contract is not the alternative to the cage. It is the cage's mirror image, and it produces a captivity of its own that we have not yet learned to name. The old captivity was the inability to leave. The new captivity is the inability to stay. We have produced a generation that cannot remain, that flees at the first sustained discomfort because it has been catechized to read discomfort as evidence of a broken machine. Stanley Hauerwas put the knife in with one sentence that has never left me. You always marry the wrong person, he wrote, and he was serious enough about it to call it a law (Hauerwas 1978). His point is not pessimism. His point is that you cannot possibly know, at the altar, who you are marrying, because neither of you is finished, and the person you wake up next to in year fifteen is someone the person at the altar never met. The contract assumes you can know your counterparty and price the deal. Marriage assumes you cannot, and binds you to the stranger anyway, which is the only condition under which two people are ever actually changed.

> The old captivity was the inability to leave. The new captivity is the inability to stay.

## The Reversal

This is the reversal, and it is the hinge of the whole thing. We have been told that marriage is supposed to make us happy, and we should ask why, then, marriage so often does not, and whether the failure is in the marriage or in the expectation. Gary Thomas asked the question that reorders everything. What if God designed marriage to make us holy more than to make us happy (Thomas 2000). I do not raise that to bless misery, and Thomas does not either. I raise it because the contract model has no category for it. A contract that does not make you happy is a contract you terminate. But a covenant that does not make you happy might be doing the deepest work it was ever going to do, sanding off the self-protection you brought to the altar, exposing the parts of you that only another person living too close could ever find. The unhappiness is not always the signal to leave. Sometimes it is the friction of two selves being made into one flesh, and the friction is the point. Tim Keller said the same in a different key, that the goal of marriage is not to spare you from suffering but to make you, through love and truth, into the person God designed you to be (Keller 2011).

> Sometimes it is the friction of two selves being made into one flesh, and the friction is the point.

But I refuse to let this stay clean, because the skeptic's history is still standing in the room, and the cage was real. So here is the line I will not cross, and the church must not cross it either. A covenant is not a sentence to suffer harm. The man who beats his wife has already broken the covenant. He shattered the one flesh long before she names it. To tell a battered woman that her vow obligates her to remain inside the violence is not covenant theology. It is the institution feeding on the person it was meant to shelter, and it is a blasphemy, and I have watched the church commit it and call the cruelty faithfulness. Covenant does not mean endure all things at any cost. It means the bond is not yours to cancel for convenience, and the difference between convenience and a covenant already broken by the other is not always easy, but it is real, and pastors who refuse to learn it have blood on their hands.

## What the Marriage Was Always Pointing At

With that guarded, I can say the rest. The Christian claim is not finally that you should choose covenant because it works better, though I think it does. The Christian claim is that marriage was never primarily about the two people at all. The Apostle takes the one flesh of Genesis and says the thing that breaks the frame open. This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:32 ESV). Every covenant marriage is a small enacted picture of a prior covenant, the one where God binds himself to a people who will fail him, and does not exit. That is the model. Not two parties protecting themselves with an agreement. One party giving himself up for the other while the other was still in the wrong. He did not write a contract with humanity that specified the conditions of his departure. He held fast. He let his defenses fall, all the way to a cross, and the holding fast is the love, and the love is the covenant, and the covenant is the thing the marriage was always pointing at.

Which means the cross does real work inside the actual body of an actual marriage, not as a metaphor but as a pattern you can practice on a Tuesday. The law comes first and it is severe. You vowed to hold fast, and holding fast will cost you the very self-protection you have spent your life building, and there are mornings the law will demand from you a death you do not feel like dying. There is no grace that skips that. But the grace is this. The God who asks you to die to yourself in your marriage is the God who died to himself first, and he does not ask the second flesh to do what the first Flesh refused to do. The covenant is not a cage he locks you in from outside. It is a death he already walked through ahead of you, and the only kind of love that has ever been worth the name has always been on the far side of exactly that death.

The woman left my office that day undecided, and I will not pretend the story resolved, because the ones that matter rarely do. But I told her one thing before she went. I told her that the question was not whether she was happy. The question was what she had promised, and to whom, and whether she believed the One she promised it before had ever, even once, walked out on her. A contract asks what you are owed. A covenant asks what you swore. The wedding you attended last summer used the words of the second and meant the first, and that gap, multiplied across a culture, is the quiet catastrophe of how we love now. We kept the vow and lost the thing the vow was for. We can have it back. But not cheaply, and not as a contract, and not without the death.

### Works Cited

Berry, Wendell. Sex, Economy, Freedom and Community. New York: Pantheon Books, 1992.

Hauerwas, Stanley. 'Sex and Politics: Bertrand Russell and Human Sexuality.' Christian Century, April 19, 1978, 417 to 422.

Keller, Timothy. The Meaning of Marriage. New York: Dutton, 2011.

Lasch, Christopher. Haven in a Heartless World. New York: Basic Books, 1977.

Thomas, Gary. Sacred Marriage. Grand Rapids: Zondervan, 2000.

title: How to Raise Children in the Faith Without Crushing Them
excerpt: The opposite of crushing a child into the faith is not letting them choose freely from a neutral distance, because there is no neutral distance, and the home is forming them whether you intend it or not.
body:
One of my sons told me, somewhere around fourteen, that he was not sure he believed any of it. He said it at the dinner table, watching my face, and I understood that he was not reporting a conclusion. He was running a test. He wanted to know whether the love in that house was load-bearing or conditional, whether the faith we had given him was a gift or a fence. I have five sons, and I have learned that the question under most of their questions is that one. Not is it true. Will you still have me if I doubt it.

The fear that drives this essay is real and I share it. We have all watched it happen. The child raised in the strict Christian home who walks out at nineteen and does not come back, who describes the faith of his childhood as something he survived rather than received. We are terrified of producing that child, and the terror makes us do one of two things, and both of them are wrong, and I have done both.

## The Two Failures the Fear Produces

The first thing the terror does is make us clamp down. We control the inputs, monitor the friends, demand the right answers, and treat every flicker of doubt as a fire to be stamped out before it spreads. We confuse compliance with formation. We raise a child who knows the answers and has never once been allowed to ask the question, and we call that success right up until the day it detonates.

The second thing the terror does is the modern correction, and it is more respectable, so it is more dangerous. We decide we will not impose anything. We will expose the child to options and let them choose for themselves when they are old enough, from a position of neutrality, free of our pressure. This sounds humble. It sounds like respect for the child's autonomy. And it is built on a lie about how human beings are actually formed.

## The Lie of the Neutral Clearing

The strongest version of the second view deserves a fair hearing, because the people who hold it are not fools and they are often refugees from the first error. They say that faith coerced is not faith, that a belief installed by parental pressure is not the child's own and will not survive contact with the world, that the only faith worth having is one freely chosen by an adult who could have chosen otherwise. They are right that coerced faith is not faith. I will not soften that, because it is true, and the church's history of producing hollow compliance is a real indictment we have earned. Where they are wrong is in the word neutral. They imagine that if they simply withhold their own convictions, the child will arrive at adulthood as a free agent in a clearing, weighing the options. But there is no clearing. There never was.

James K.A. Smith has spent his career arguing the thing parents most need to hear and least want to believe. We are not primarily thinking beings who occasionally feel. We are loving beings, formed less by what we are taught than by what we practice, shaped at a level beneath cognition by the habits and rhythms and liturgies we are immersed in (Smith 2009). Your child is being formed every day, by something, toward some vision of the good life. The question is never whether your child is being discipled. The question is only by what. The home that withholds its convictions in the name of neutrality has not created a neutral space. It has simply handed the formation to whatever else is in the room, and there is always something else in the room, and most of it is selling.

> The question is never whether your child is being discipled. The question is only by what.

The dream of the neutral clearing has a traceable history, and naming it helps, because an idea you can date is an idea you can stop obeying. It begins in earnest with Rousseau, whose Emile in 1762 imagined a child raised away from the corruptions of inherited belief so that his nature could unfold on its own, and the picture was beautiful and it was a fiction, because no child has ever been raised in nature alone. The fiction crossed the Atlantic and hardened into method. By the middle of the twentieth century the child-rearing experts had professionalized it, and after Benjamin Spock published his manual in 1946 a generation of American parents absorbed the conviction that the good parent steps back, supplies options, and lets the child's own self emerge undirected. The screen and the school did not invent the neutral ideal. They inherited it from two centuries of believing that formation is something we do to a child rather than something always already happening, and then they filled the clearing the theory pretended was empty.

So the choice was never between forming your child and leaving them free. That choice does not exist. The choice is between forming them on purpose and forming them by accident, between a household with an intentional shape and a household whose shape is set by the default liturgies of the screen and the school and the market. Once you see that, the whole question changes. It is no longer how do I avoid imposing. It is what am I immersing them in, and is it true, and is it warm, and can it hold their weight.

## Formation in the Geography of a Shared Life

Let me carry one text through this. Moses, instructing a whole people on how to hand faith to the next generation, does not say enroll them in a class. He says these words shall be on your heart, and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise (Deuteronomy 6:6 to 7 ESV). Read it slowly. The faith is transmitted in the ordinary geography of a shared life. Sitting, walking, lying down, rising. It is not a curriculum. It is a texture. And notice the first clause, the one we skip. These words shall be on your heart. The instruction to the parent precedes the instruction about the child. You cannot talk of them by the way if they are not on your heart, because children do not absorb what you teach. They absorb what you are. The reason so much religious upbringing produces refugees is that the words were on the schedule and never on the heart, and children can smell the difference from across a house.

This is where the crushing happens, and it is worth naming precisely. A child is crushed not by the presence of faith in the home but by the presence of a faith that is performed rather than possessed, demanded rather than displayed. When the rules are enforced but the joy is absent, when the doctrine is defended but the love is rationed, the child concludes, correctly, that this thing is about control and not about life. They are not rejecting Christ when they leave. They never met him. They met an enforcement mechanism wearing his name, and they were right to flee it, and we should be careful before we call their leaving rebellion when it was sometimes just honesty.

> They are not rejecting Christ when they leave. They never met him.

## A Home That Forms Without Crushing

So what does the home look like that forms without crushing. I want to give you the pattern, not as tips, because the pattern is the point. First, the doubt has to be welcome at the table. When my son said he was not sure he believed, the single most important thing was that nothing in my face changed. The home that punishes doubt teaches the child to hide it, and a hidden doubt does not die, it goes underground and grows in the dark and comes back at nineteen with a moving van. The home that welcomes the doubt says the truth can survive your questions, and a child who learns that the faith is not afraid of his hardest question is a child who has been handed something durable. I told my son that I had not believed any of it once either, that I came to all of this from the outside, from atheism, and that his question was not a betrayal of our house but the oldest question in it.

Second, the practices have to be real before they are explained. Smith's whole argument is that we are shaped by what we do before we are shaped by what we are told, and this means the family that prays together, eats together, confesses to each other, and keeps the rhythms of the church year is forming the child's loves at a depth no argument will reach. Not because the practices are magic, but because they are the soil. You are not installing beliefs. You are tilling ground, and beliefs grow in tilled ground or they do not grow at all. The child raised inside genuine practice has a body that knows how to pray before he has decided whether prayer is reasonable, and that bodily knowledge is what carries him through the years when the arguments wobble.

Third, and this is the one that costs, the faith has to be allowed to become theirs, which means it has to be allowed to look different from yours. The goal of raising a child in the faith is not a copy of you. It is a person who has met God for themselves, and a person who has met God for themselves will have edges you did not put there, convictions you did not hand them, a relationship with the same Lord that does not route through your approval. The parent who needs the child's faith to validate their own will crush the child every time, because they will read every divergence as a loss. You are not raising a believer who agrees with you. You are raising a person who belongs to God, and those are not the same project, and confusing them is how the strict home and the controlling home do their damage.

## The Law and the Grace of Handing Down Faith

There is a law in this before there is grace, and I will not skip it. The law is that you cannot give what you do not have. A child cannot be immersed in a love of God that the parent does not actually possess, and no technique closes that gap. If the faith is not on your heart, your children will inherit the performance and not the thing, and you will have taught them, with your life, that this is a script people run and not a Lord people love. That is the severe word and there is no way around it. The grace is that you do not have to be finished to be faithful. My sons did not need a father with no doubts. They needed a father who let them watch him bring his doubts to God instead of hiding them, who failed in front of them and repented in front of them and prayed in front of them as a man who needed it. Children are not formed by parents who have arrived. They are formed by parents who are honestly on the way, and who let themselves be seen on it.

My son who said he was not sure is older now, and I will not tell you the story ended in a tidy profession of faith, because I do not get to script that and neither do you, and any essay that promises you the formula is selling you the very control that does the crushing. What I will tell you is that he still comes home, and the faith is still on the table between us, doubts and all, and the love never once became the weapon. We do not get to guarantee the outcome. We were never told we would. We were told to put the words on our own hearts first and then talk of them by the way, and to make a home warm enough and true enough that when the hard years come, the child has somewhere to bring the doubt instead of somewhere to run from. That is the whole assignment. The rest belongs to God, and it always did, and the parents who could not bear that it belonged to God are the ones who tried to do God's part with their fists.

> We do not get to guarantee the outcome. We were never told we would.

### Works Cited

Rousseau, Jean-Jacques. Emile, or On Education. 1762. Translated by Allan Bloom. New York: Basic Books, 1979.

Smith, James K.A. Desiring the Kingdom. Grand Rapids: Baker Academic, 2009.

Spock, Benjamin. The Common Sense Book of Baby and Child Care. New York: Duell, Sloan and Pearce, 1946.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

title: What Fatherhood Requires
excerpt: We have spent a generation telling fathers to be present, and presence is necessary and nowhere near sufficient, because a man can be in the room and still hand his children nothing.
body:
A father came to me after a service, a good man by every external measure, and told me he was doing everything his own father had not. He was there. He coached the team, attended the recitals, made the dinners, never missed a thing. And he said it with a kind of exhaustion underneath the pride, because something was not working and he could not name it, and he wanted me to tell him what more there could possibly be when he had already given everything his absent father withheld. I knew what he was feeling, and I told him the truth, which is that presence is the floor and he had mistaken it for the house.

We have spent a generation correcting a real failure. The absent father, checked out or gone, is a wound this culture knows intimately, and the call to presence was right and I will not take it back. But the correction has curdled into a ceiling. We told men that fatherhood means being there, and a great many men have heard that and concluded that physical and emotional attendance is the whole of the job. They show up to the events. They are kind. And they hand their children, year after year, no account of what a life is for, no transmitted weight, no formed conscience, no God. They are present and empty, and the children grow up well-attended and unformed, and we have not yet found the language to tell those fathers that they are failing, because by the only metric we gave them they are succeeding.

> But the correction has curdled into a ceiling.

## Presence as Floor, Not House

So I want to ask what fatherhood actually requires, beyond the floor. And I want to put the strongest objection first. There is a serious case, made by serious people, that the whole category of distinctly paternal authority is a relic we are better off retiring, that it has historically been a license for domination, that children need love and safety and not some gendered transmission of weight from a man positioned above them. The case points to every father who used the word authority to mean tyranny, every household where the father's word was law because the father's fist enforced it. And the case is right about all of that. The history of fatherhood is full of men who confused the office with ownership and ruled their homes as small kingdoms of fear.

## How the Father Was Pulled From the Home

But the empty father the objection accidentally blesses has a history too, and it can be dated. For most of the agrarian world the father worked within sight of his children, and the farm or the workshop was the classroom where a son learned a trade and a way of being a man from a man he watched all day. The Industrial Revolution of the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries pulled that father out of the home and into the factory and the office, and for the first time work and fatherhood were done in separate buildings. The father became a provider who left at dawn and returned at dark, and the daily transmission that the shared work had carried was severed. By the time the child-rearing experts professionalized American parenthood in the mid twentieth century, the father had already been reduced in the culture to a wallet and a disciplinarian, present mainly as an absence. The merely present father is not the opposite of that history. He is its latest form, a man who came back into the home physically and found he no longer had a way to hand anything down, because the structure that used to do it for him was demolished two centuries ago and never rebuilt.

Where the objection goes wrong is in concluding that because the thing was abused, the thing itself was the abuse. The father who dominates and the father who is merely present are not opposites. They are the same failure facing different directions. Both have refused the actual office, which is neither to rule the child nor to befriend the child but to form the child, to hand down a way of being human that the child can stand on. The tyrant deformed instead of formed. The merely present father forms nothing at all, and leaves the child to be formed by whatever else is bidding. The objection correctly rejects the tyrant and then accidentally blesses the empty man, and the empty man is doing quieter damage in far more homes.

## The Office Paul Names

Let me carry one text. Paul writes to a church he founded and reaches for the image that says what he means, and the image is fatherhood. We exhorted each one of you, he writes, like a father with his children, to walk in a manner worthy of God (1 Thessalonians 2:11 to 12 ESV). Sit with the verbs around that image, because Paul lists three. Earlier in the passage he says he was gentle among them like a nursing mother, and then this, the father who exhorts and encourages and charges. Exhort, encourage, charge. Not provide, attend, and stay out of the way. The paternal office in that sentence is active and directional. It points the child somewhere. It says walk in this manner and not that one, toward this God and not that idol. The father is doing something to the child's sense of the good, handing over a direction. That is the requirement the floor cannot reach. Presence puts you in the room. Only formation hands the child a way to walk once you are gone.

Now watch the warning Paul gives elsewhere, because it guards the office from becoming the tyranny the skeptic feared. Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4 ESV). Both clauses are commands and they are aimed at the same man. The father is told to instruct, to discipline, to hand down, and in the same breath told that he can do this in a way that provokes and embitters, and that he must not. The text refuses both errors at once. It will not let the father abdicate the formation, and it will not let him perform the formation in a way that crushes. The empty father has dropped the second clause's content. The tyrant has dropped its restraint. The office lives in holding both, and holding both is hard, which is why so few men do it, which is why we keep producing tyrants and ghosts and almost nothing in between.

> The empty father has dropped the second clause's content. The tyrant has dropped its restraint.

## What the Office Actually Requires

So what does the office require, concretely. It requires, first, that you have a way of being human to hand down, which means you have to have done the work of becoming a person yourself. A father cannot transmit a weight he does not carry. The reason so many present fathers form nothing is that they have nothing formed to give, no examined account of what a life is for, no faith they actually hold, no conscience they have actually built. They were never handed it either, often, and the chain of empty men runs back further than any of them can see. To break it, a man has to become the kind of person worth imitating, and there is no shortcut, and the absence of the shortcut is the whole difficulty. You do not father out of techniques. You father out of who you have become, and your children read who you have become with a precision that would terrify you if you let yourself feel it.

It requires, second, that you actually exercise the directional office, that you tell your children what a life is for and aim them at it, with words and not only by osmosis. The merely present father trusts that good attendance will somehow diffuse into good formation, and it does not, because formation is active. Children need to be told, in words, what is worth living for, what is worth refusing, what God asks of a person and why. Not nagged. Charged, the way Paul says, with the weight of a man who believes what he is handing over. The father who never says it out loud, who only attends, has decided that the most important things will be transmitted by accident, and the most important things are never transmitted by accident.

It requires, third, the willingness to be disliked in the short term for the sake of the child in the long term, and this is where the empty father most often fails, because attendance is pleasant and formation is not always. To hand a child a conscience is to constrain the child, and the child will resent the constraint, and the father who needs his children to like him every day cannot do the job. This is not the tyrant's coldness. It is its opposite. It is love willing to spend its own popularity, willing to be the bad guy on a Tuesday so the child has something to stand on at forty. The father who cannot bear his child's momentary anger will, to avoid it, withhold exactly the formation the child most needs, and call the withholding kindness.

## The Father Seen Failing and Returning

Here is the reversal, and it is the heart of the thing. We assume the strong father is the one with answers, the finished man who hands down certainty from a height. But the fatherhood that actually forms is the one willing to be seen failing and repenting in front of the child, because the deepest thing a father transmits is not a set of rules but a way of being a sinner before God. My sons have not been formed most by my instruction. They have been formed most by watching me get it wrong, name it, and turn around, because that is the actual shape of the Christian life, and a father who only ever displays competence hands his children a lie about what walking with God looks like. The strongest thing I have ever given them is the sight of their father on his knees about his own failure. That is not weakness in the office. That is the office at its fullest, because it hands down the one thing they will need most, which is how to fall and return.

## Law and Grace at the Center of the Office

The cross does the work here, law before grace, and the law is heavy. The requirement is that you become a man worth imitating and then actively hand down a way to live, and most of us are not that man and did not receive that handing, and the law exposes the gap without mercy. There is no version of this you can fake. Your children will inherit who you actually are, not who you instruct them to be, and that is a sentence of judgment on every father including me. But the grace is the same grace that is always underneath the law. The Father this whole office images did not father from a safe height. He handed over his own Son, gave him up for children who were in open rebellion, and the model of fatherhood at the center of the faith is a Father whose love cost him everything and a Son who handed down the way to live by walking it to a grave and out the other side. You are not asked to father out of your own sufficiency. You are asked to father as a man who has himself been fathered by that God, and the having-been-fathered is the only soil the office grows in.

The man who came to me after the service was not a failure. He was a man who had climbed out of one pit and stopped at the rim, thinking the rim was the summit. I told him to keep going. Attendance got you here, I said, and now your children need to know what you are for, and they cannot read it off your calendar. They need to hear it, and watch you hold it, and watch you fail at it and return to it, until the thing is on their bones the way it is on yours. Presence is where fatherhood starts. It was never where it was allowed to stop. We told a generation of men to be there, and they came, and now we owe them the harder word. Being there is not the gift. Being there is the cost of admission to the work of handing your children a way to be human, and the work is still in front of you, and it always was.

> Being there is not the gift. Being there is the cost of admission to the work of handing your children a way to be human, and the work is still in front of you, and it always was.

### Works Cited

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

title: Protecting Your Marriage From the Demands of Work
excerpt: Work does not steal your marriage by being evil, it steals it by being good, by giving you the clear scoreboard and visible reward that marriage withholds, until you are quietly more married to the job.
body:
A man told me, with no apparent grief, that his marriage had become a logistics partnership. He and his wife coordinated children and calendars and money with great efficiency, and they had not had a real conversation in months, and he reported this the way you would report the weather, because nothing dramatic had gone wrong. No affair. No fight. The marriage had simply been crowded out, one good and urgent work demand at a time, until what remained was a smooth-running operation with two strangers at the controls. He had not chosen against his wife on any single day. He had chosen against her on a thousand days so small that none of them felt like a choice.

This is how work takes a marriage, and the reason it is hard to fight is that work does not present itself as the enemy. The affair is obvious. You can repent of an affair. But how do you repent of being responsible. How do you name the problem when the problem is that you provided, that you answered the email, that you took the meeting, that you did the thing everyone praised you for doing. Work does not seduce a marriage by being a vice. It seduces by being a virtue, and a virtue is much harder to resist than a vice, because you feel righteous the whole time you are losing the thing that matters most.

> It seduces by being a virtue, and a virtue is much harder to resist than a vice, because you feel righteous the whole time you are losing the thing that matters most.

## When Provision Becomes the Cover

Let me give the strongest version of the counterargument, because there is one and it is not stupid. The objection says that providing for your family is itself an act of love, that the man or woman grinding at a demanding job is not neglecting the marriage but serving it, building the security and the future the family depends on, and that the soft talk about presence and connection is a luxury belief held by people who have never worried about rent. Work is how you love them, the objection says. The paycheck is the affection in usable form. And there is real truth in that, enough that I will not wave it away. Provision is love. The parent working a double shift to keep the lights on is not failing the family, they are carrying it, and any pastor who lectures that parent about quality time has never been poor and should sit down.

Where the objection fails is in the slide it permits, the slide from work is a way of loving them to work is the way of loving them, and from there to a place where the providing has entirely replaced the presence and the provider tells himself the replacement is the gift. The man in my office was not poor. His extra hours were not keeping the lights on. They were buying a slightly larger house and a great deal of esteem, and he had wrapped the whole thing in the language of provision because provision is the respectable name for it. The honest provision the objection defends and the quiet abandonment I am describing can look identical from outside, and the difference is whether the work is serving the marriage or has become the rival the marriage now serves. Most of us cannot tell which we are doing, because the same activity hosts both, and we always narrate ourselves as the provider and never as the deserter.

## Work Was Never the Cure for Aloneness

Let me carry one text. In the second creation account, before any work goes wrong, God puts the man in the garden to work it and keep it (Genesis 2:15 ESV), and then immediately declares that it is not good for the man to be alone and makes the woman, and the order matters. Work comes first in the text and the marriage comes second, but the marriage is the thing declared not good to be without. Work is given as a vocation and it is genuinely good. The one flesh is given as the answer to a lack that work could not fill, because the man in the garden was already working and still alone, and his aloneness was not solved by more garden. Here is the diagnostic the text hands us. If you are working harder and lonelier, you are repeating the man's pre-marriage condition inside your marriage, surrounded by good labor and still unaccompanied, and no amount of additional good labor will touch it, because labor was never the cure for aloneness. It was the context the cure was given into.

The contest I am describing is not timeless, though it feels that way, and naming when it sharpened helps. For most of human history work and marriage occupied the same ground. The household was the workplace, the farm and the shop were where the couple labored side by side, and there was no commute between the two because there was no distance to cross. The Industrial Revolution of the nineteenth century pried them apart, pulling work out of the home and into the factory and the office, and once work happened somewhere the marriage could not see, the two became rivals for the same hours instead of partners in the same labor. The man who told me his marriage was a logistics partnership is living in the architecture that separation built. He leaves the marriage every morning to go to the place where work is, and the leaving is so normal that he never notices he is choosing one location over the other, every day, by reflex. The scoreboard I am about to describe got its power from that arrangement, because once the work moved out of sight, it was the only one of the two that came home with a number attached.

## Why the Scoreboard Wins

The reason work wins, practically, is that it offers what marriage by its nature withholds. Work gives you a scoreboard. There are deadlines met, numbers hit, projects shipped, promotions granted, a steady stream of visible evidence that you are competent and that you matter. Marriage offers no such scoreboard. The work of marriage is mostly invisible, rarely rewarded in any legible way, and never finished. So when a person is starving for the feeling of competence, and most of us are, work feeds them and marriage does not, and they drift toward the thing that feeds them, and they call the drift ambition. The cruelest part is that the better you are at your work, the stronger the pull, because the rewards are richer and the scoreboard lights up brighter, and the marriage, which never lights up at all, recedes by comparison until it is a logistics partnership and you did not even feel it go.

> The marriage will never out-shout the job. It cannot.

So the protection of a marriage from work is not finally about time management, though it involves time. It is about correctly identifying what is happening, which is a contest between two things competing for the center of your life, one of which announces its claims loudly with deadlines and one of which makes its claims silently and loses every loud contest by default. The marriage will never out-shout the job. It cannot. It does not have the volume. Which means the only way it survives is if you decide, in advance and against the noise, that it sits at the center and the work serves it, and then you defend that decision on the small days when nothing seems to be at stake, because the small days are the only days there ever are.

## Defending the Center in Calm Weather

What does the defense look like, concretely. It looks, first, like protected unproductive time, hours given to the marriage that produce nothing and prove nothing, where you are not solving a logistics problem together but simply present to each other with no scoreboard running. This will feel like a waste to a person trained by work, and the feeling that it is a waste is precisely the disease. The most important time in a marriage is time that accomplishes nothing measurable, and a person who can only justify time by its output has already been colonized by the logic of the job, and the marriage is dying of efficiency.

It looks, second, like a hard limit you set when no crisis demands it, a place where the work is told no on principle and not on emergency. The man who waits for a work demand extreme enough to justify refusing it will never refuse anything, because the demands are individually always reasonable. You stop the encroachment by drawing the line in calm weather, by deciding that this evening, this day, this season is not available to the job, and holding it when the job comes asking politely with a request that is, taken alone, entirely fair. The fairness of each individual request is the mechanism of the loss. You defeat it only by refusing on grounds that precede the request.

It looks, third, like telling the truth about what your work is actually buying, because the provision story is sometimes true and sometimes a cover, and only you and God know which. Eugene Peterson spent his life warning pastors that busyness is not a sign of devotion but a sign of disordered loves, that the busy person is usually busy because being busy is the way they avoid the harder and quieter work of actually being present to the people in front of them (Peterson 1989). His warning was to pastors but it indicts all of us. Ask whether your hours are feeding your family or feeding your need to feel important, and refuse the easy answer, because the easy answer is always provision and the true answer is sometimes vanity wearing provision's coat.

## The Deeper Theft of the Imagination

Here is the reversal. We protect our marriages from work as though the threat were that work will take our time, and time is part of it, but the deeper theft is that work will reshape what we think a person is for. Spend enough years in a world that measures you by output and rewards you by results, and you will start, without deciding to, treating your spouse as a project to be managed rather than a person to be known, applying to the marriage the only logic you have left, the logic of efficiency and return. The man with the logistics partnership had not just given his hours to the job. He had given the job his imagination, and it had taught him to see his wife as a coordination problem, and that deformation of his seeing was the real damage, deeper than any missed dinner.

## The Law and the Reordering of Loves

The cross does the work, and the law comes first, severe and exact. Genesis put the marriage at the center as the answer to aloneness and you have let a good thing climb up and take that center, and you cannot serve two masters, and the master you actually serve is the one you reorganize your real life around, not the one you praise on Sunday. By that measure many of us are married to our work and merely cohabiting with our spouse, and the law says so plainly and gives no relief. But the grace is that the God who put the man in the garden to work it is the same God who declared his aloneness not good and gave him another, and that God does not ask you to abandon your work to save your marriage. He asks you to put it back in its place, under the marriage and not over it, and the One who orders all loves rightly is willing to reorder yours, beginning the moment you stop calling the disorder provision and name it for what it is.

The man left and did not change overnight, because no one does, and the marriage that erodes over a thousand small days is rebuilt the same way, a thousand small days back. But he started by admitting that the logistics partnership was not the accidental residue of responsibility. It was the predictable result of a contest he had been losing for years without knowing a contest was on. Work did not steal his marriage by being bad. It stole it by being good, and by being loud, and by being where the scoreboard was, and he had wandered toward the lights like everyone does. The marriage was still there, quiet in the dark where he had left it, waiting to be chosen on a day when nothing forced the choice. That is the only kind of day there is. Choose it then, or you will not choose it at all.

> Work did not steal his marriage by being bad. It stole it by being good, and by being loud, and by being where the scoreboard was, and he had wandered toward the lights like everyone does.

### Works Cited

Peterson, Eugene H. The Contemplative Pastor. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1989.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

title: Forgiveness in Marriage: How to Actually Do It
excerpt: Forgiveness is not the feeling that the wound no longer hurts, it is the decision to absorb a cost yourself instead of making the other person keep paying, and that is why it feels like dying, because it is.
body:
A couple sat in my office keeping a ledger they would have denied keeping. Every grievance was filed, dated, and available for instant retrieval, and when one of them named an old hurt, the other produced a matching one from the archive, and the conversation was not a fight so much as an audit. They had been wounding each other for years and forgiving each other never, and they had mistaken the not-divorcing for forgiveness, when in fact they were simply two creditors who had agreed not to call in the debt while never once forgiving it. The debt sat there, accruing interest, and the marriage was paying it down with everything good in them.

This is the most common condition I see in long marriages, and it is not dramatic, which is why it is so dangerous. Nothing has blown up. They are still together. But the accumulated unforgiveness has turned the marriage into a cold accounting, two people who have each been hurt enough times to hold a grudge in permanent reserve, deploying it whenever the other gets close enough to matter. They do not need to learn to fight better. They need to learn to forgive, and they do not know how, because no one ever told them what forgiveness actually is, and most of what they have heard about it is false.

> They do not need to learn to fight better. They need to learn to forgive, and they do not know how, because no one ever told them what forgiveness actually is, and most of what they have heard about it is false.

## The False Account of Forgiveness

The false account says forgiveness is a feeling, that you have forgiven when the hurt stops hurting and the warmth returns, and that until the feeling arrives you would be a hypocrite to claim forgiveness. This sounds honest. It is paralyzing. It makes forgiveness something that happens to you rather than something you do, and it leaves you waiting for an emotional weather change that may never come, while the wound stays open and the ledger keeps growing. The person waiting to feel forgiving will wait forever, and the marriage dies in the waiting room.

## How Forgiveness Became a Feeling

This idea that forgiveness is a feeling did not fall out of the sky, and it is younger than we assume. For most of Christian history forgiveness was understood as an act, a thing you did and even owed, modeled on a God who pardons by decree. The shift to forgiveness-as-emotion belongs to a particular and traceable turn. Philip Rieff named it in 1966, when he argued that the modern West had quietly replaced the older moral order with a therapeutic one, a culture in which the inner self and its feelings became the final measure of what is real and the management of those feelings became the new salvation (Rieff 1966). On that account forgiveness stops being something you grant the offender and becomes something you do for your own emotional relief, a private adjustment of your interior weather, and it is not complete until you feel better. We absorbed that reframing without noticing, and it hollowed the word out. The couple in my office were waiting for a feeling to arrive because they had inherited, from a culture sixty years deep in this turn, the conviction that the feeling was the thing. It is not the thing. It never was.

The strongest objection to everything I am about to say comes from people who have watched forgiveness used as a weapon, and they are not wrong. They have seen the abused spouse told to forgive and stay, the pattern of harm laundered through cheap grace, the word forgiveness deployed by the church to pressure victims back into danger and to spare offenders the consequences they had earned. They conclude that forgiveness talk in marriage is suspect, that it serves power, that it asks the wounded to absorb what the wounding party should have to answer for. I grant every case they cite, and I grant it without flinching, because the church has done this and called it holy, and it is a sin against the wounded that I have watched up close. Forgiveness has been weaponized, and a theology of forgiveness that cannot distinguish itself from enabling is a theology that has armed abusers.

## Forgiveness Is Not Reconciliation

But the objection proves too much, because it assumes forgiveness means the cancellation of consequences and the restoration of trust, and it does not mean either of those. This is the distinction that changes everything. Forgiveness is not reconciliation. Forgiveness is unilateral, something you can do alone, the decision to stop requiring the other person to pay for what they did. Reconciliation is bilateral, requires repentance and changed behavior and rebuilt trust, and may rightly never come if the offense continues. You can forgive a person you do not trust. You can forgive a person from a safe distance you have every right to keep. The abused spouse can forgive in the heart and still flee the danger and still let the consequences fall, because forgiveness was never the surrender of safety. It was only the release of the debt, and releasing the debt does not mean handing the offender the keys.

## The King Who Absorbed the Debt

Let me carry one text, the one Jesus made the hinge of the whole thing. After the great parable of the servant forgiven an unpayable debt who then seizes a fellow servant by the throat over a small one, the warning lands. So also my heavenly Father will do to every one of you, if you do not forgive your brother from your heart (Matthew 18:35 ESV). The parable defines forgiveness precisely, and we miss it because we know the story too well. The king forgives a debt. He does not feel better about the servant. He does not restore warm relations. He absorbs the loss. That is the whole of it. The servant owed a sum he could never repay, and the king, instead of extracting it, ate the cost himself. Forgiveness is the king's decision to take the loss onto his own books rather than make the debtor keep paying. Translate that into a marriage and you have the only definition that works. To forgive your spouse is to absorb the cost of what they did to you, to carry it yourself, instead of making them carry it forever in the form of your withdrawn affection and your retrievable grudge.

That is why forgiveness feels like dying, because it is a kind of dying. The debt is real. The hurt genuinely cost you something, and forgiveness does not pretend otherwise, does not say it was fine or it did not matter. It says it mattered, it cost me, and I am going to pay the cost myself rather than charge it to you for the rest of our lives. Someone always pays for a wound. The only question is who. Unforgiveness makes the offender pay, in installments, forever, which is what the couple in my office were doing to each other, two people each insisting the other keep paying, both of them broke. Forgiveness ends the collection by absorbing the loss, and absorbing a loss is never free and never painless, and anyone who told you forgiveness was easy was describing something else, probably denial.

> Someone always pays for a wound. The only question is who.

## How You Actually Do It

So how do you actually do it, because the couple in my office did not need a definition, they needed a way out of the audit. It begins, first, with the decision that precedes the feeling. You forgive as an act of the will before you forgive as a condition of the heart, the way the king canceled the debt by decree and not by sentiment. You decide to stop bringing the offense up, to stop deploying it, to stop charging the other person interest on it, and you make that decision while the wound still hurts, because the decision is what eventually drains the hurt and not the other way around. The feeling follows the decision by a road that is sometimes long, but it never once leads, and the person waiting for it to lead waits forever.

It requires, second, the surrender of the ledger, and this is the specific death the couple in my office most needed to die. The retrievable grudge, the filed and dated grievance available for redeployment, has to be actually destroyed and not merely set down where you can pick it up again. As long as you keep the offense in reserve, you have not forgiven it, you have only postponed the collection, and your spouse can feel the file in the room even when you do not open it. Hauerwas observed that marriage requires a peculiar kind of forgiveness because we always marry the wrong person and then spend the marriage being married to a person who keeps changing into someone we did not agree to (Hauerwas 1978). You will be wounded by a stranger you did not sign up for, repeatedly, over decades, and a marriage survives only if forgiveness is a renewable practice and not a one-time event, only if you are willing to keep tearing up the ledger that keeps reassembling itself.

## The Grudge That Imprisons the One Who Holds It

Here is the reversal, and it is the thing the couple could not see. They each believed their unforgiveness was a form of self-protection, that holding the grudge kept them safe from being hurt again, that releasing it would leave them defenseless. But the unforgiveness was not protecting them. It was the wound. The grudge does not guard the one who holds it. It poisons him, keeps the injury permanently fresh by refusing to let it close, ties the holder to the very offense he resents by making him relive it on demand. They thought they were defended. They were imprisoned, each chained to the other's worst moments by the refusal to release them, and the release they feared as surrender was the only door out of the cell. Forgiveness does not make you a victim again. It is the one move that stops the original wound from going on victimizing you forever through your own hand.

## The Cross Is Not the Example, It Is the Supply

The cross does the work, and the law comes first with no anesthetic. The standard Jesus sets is that you forgive from the heart as you have been forgiven, and the parable's warning is that the one who will not release a small debt while having been released an infinite one has not understood his own forgiveness at all. That is the law and it is crushing, because measured against it every grudge I hold is the forgiven servant grabbing a throat, and I have held plenty, and so have you. But the grace is the ground the law stands on. You are asked to absorb your spouse's debt because a King absorbed yours, took the unpayable sum onto his own books at the cross and ate the loss himself rather than make you pay it. You do not forgive out of your own reserves of magnanimity, which are thin and run out fast. You forgive as a person who has been forgiven so far past your capacity to repay that the grudges you are clutching look, in that light, exactly like the small change they are. The cross is not the example. It is the supply.

The couple in my office did not lay down the ledger that day, because a habit built over fifteen years does not dissolve in an hour, and I would distrust any story where it did. But one of them said something near the end that cracked the thing open. He said he was tired of being the creditor. He did not yet feel forgiving. He had simply seen, finally, that the collection was bankrupting them both, and that someone had to absorb a loss or the marriage would keep paying with everything good in it. That is where forgiveness starts, not in a feeling, but in a tired person deciding to take the loss instead of charging it, deciding to die that particular death because the alternative was watching the marriage die instead. Forgiveness will cost you. It was always going to cost you. The only question a marriage ever really asks is whether you would rather pay that cost yourself, or make the person you promised to love keep paying it until there is nothing left of either of you to collect.

### Works Cited

Hauerwas, Stanley. 'Sex and Politics: Bertrand Russell and Human Sexuality.' Christian Century, April 19, 1978, 417 to 422.

Rieff, Philip. The Triumph of the Therapeutic: Uses of Faith After Freud. New York: Harper and Row, 1966.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

> Forgiveness will cost you. It was always going to cost you.
